description: Media Arts Foundation width tiers — 4 standards, all capability strands. Generated from node_file_generation_prompt_v5.md and width_generation_prompt.md v1.0.
subject: Media Arts

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest single context that honestly meets the descriptor's command term — one task type, one medium, one audience interaction.
width_notes.typical_width: Full Foundation scope grounded in common elaboration cases — multiple modes or media encountered, ideas communicated across at least two different contexts.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment through additional task contexts: different media, different purposes, digital tools, First Nations arts connections where elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations used as source data for typical_width and to identify wider directions. Not treated as a required checklist — elaboration variants of the same activity are merged.

AC9AMAFC01.minimum_width: Create one arts work in a single form (e.g. a captured image sequence, a voice recording, or a digital retelling) that communicates a recognisable idea from personal or social experience.
AC9AMAFC01.typical_width: Create arts works across two or more forms (e.g. moving image with voice-over, soundscape with images, or puppet/object-based story) to communicate ideas from lived or imaginative experience; manipulate available materials and technologies to develop and extend ideas.
wider: Create a media arts work using digital devices (camera, tablet, recording app) with intentional sequencing — images ordered to tell a story or communicate a feeling, with added captions or sound
Devise and record a chant, rap or sound piece using voice and found objects to communicate a message or retell a story, documented via a school-managed digital platform
Create a work repurposing materials and objects (packing boxes, clothing) as environments or characters, and capture it using a digital device to share with an audience
elaborations: creating arts works in a range of forms to communicate ideas from lived personal or social experiences; for example, creating a dance or scenes showing favourite activities such as games; using digital devices to record their peers playing a game and creating a voice-over that describes what's happening; composing a song or chant about a favourite food or activity; drawing a home scene of people and animals

creating works in response to inspiration from sources such as play, imagination, observation, literature, artworks from their cultures and communities or arts knowledge and skill development activities
extending and varying known songs, chants or rhymes; for example, changing words, interpreting without using voice, adding movements/actions or improvising rhythm patterns as accompaniment
manipulating objects, puppets, 2D images and/or available technologies to create or retell stories

devising a chant/rap that a character from an animated series, a text or a fictional hero could use to communicate a health or sustainability message or to learn the steps in a process; recording the chant/rap using an available digital device and sharing live or via a school-managed space such as a learning management system

repurposing materials and objects such as clothing or packing boxes as starting points for imagining and developing scenes and scenarios; for example, using packing boxes to create an imagined environment or vehicle

considering as a class the characters and situations associated with a story and then re-imagining them by asking questions of the story, such as "What's up?", "What happens next?" or "What else might/could happen?" to support the development of their own socio-dramatic or miniature worlds play

AC9AMAFD01.minimum_width: Use play and imagination to explore one arts material, movement, or technology — discover at least one new possibility and explain what they found.
AC9AMAFD01.typical_width: Explore the possibilities of multiple materials, movement qualities, and technologies through play and experimentation; discover and describe how different choices change the ideas communicated; use imaginative questioning ('What happens next?', 'What else could happen?') to develop ideas.
wider: Explore tactile and sensory qualities of materials (rough/smooth/soft) and use movement, voice, or digital tools to embody or represent those qualities — connecting sensory discovery to idea development
Use a camera to capture a series of images documenting a process (e.g. mixing colours, building a structure), then sequence and annotate them as a record of discovery
Improvise rhythmic patterns, melodies, or movement sequences and interpret these visually using drawing or collage — cross-arts exploration as a discovery practice
elaborations: playing with the tactile qualities of a range of materials (rough, smooth, spikey, gooey) and exploring how they feel about these qualities to develop ideas for a visual artwork, dance or soundscape
imagining how the characters in a story they are reading might dress or move, and making still or moving images to communicate ideas about the characters
identifying and describing shapes, colours and lines they observe in their environment and exploring ways to use these shapes creatively

playing games to develop subject-specific practices such as pitch, beat and/or rhythm recognition; exploring ways that body parts, zones and bases can be moved safely and expressively; taking on the point of view of a fictional character in dramatic play
responding to the emotions they experience while listening to different pieces of music and using movement to share their response

improvising rhythmic patterns for clapping or stamping, or inventing new movements for familiar action songs, and interpreting these visually using elements of art/design such as shapes, lines and/or colours
exploring their speaking and singing voices and discovering ways they can use their voices/vocalisation to communicate ideas and feelings

improvising movements to explain the steps in a process, and then using a camera to capture a series of images/photographic story that can be displayed in the classroom to remind everybody about the process

AC9AMAFE01.minimum_width: Identify one type of arts work from their own life or community (e.g. a song, a cartoon, a game, a dance) and share ideas about why it is important to people.
AC9AMAFE01.typical_width: Identify and describe a range of arts works and experiences from their lives (songs, dances, animations, computer games, public art, performances) and explain how they communicate feelings, ideas and cultural knowledge; make connections between arts works and the people and communities who create or value them.
wider: Listen to and discuss stories shared by First Nations Australians about the importance of arts for connecting to people, culture and Country/Place — using resources created or co-created by First Nations Australian communities
Explore how illustrations and images in texts (picture books, screen media) communicate narrative, character and mood — connecting arts exploration to literacy contexts
Investigate how songs, chants and anthems are used for social celebrations and shared purposes (birthdays, school events, sports), and reflect on how these arts works bring communities together
elaborations: exploring how facial expressions, gestures and other ways of moving, and using voice or language, can communicate emotions and feelings in arts works
identifying and/or learning social or cultural dances that have meaning for people and communities, taking care to observe relevant protocols
using dramatic play to explore ideas or understandings they observe or perceive in a text or image

identifying arts works and experiences in their lives, such as songs they sing, dances or drama they watch or perform, animations, computer games or music videos, public art, 2D, 3D or screen-based works they encounter at school or in community settings
singing songs that are used for celebrations, such as school songs, anthems, sports teams' songs, birthday songs
exploring how illustrations/images in a text help to communicate narrative or information about characters or settings and/or mood

listening to First Nations Australians talk about the importance of the arts for connecting to people, culture and Country/Place; for example, using resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians

AC9AMAFP01.minimum_width: Share one arts work with an audience (teacher, small group, or class) and respond to at least one question about it — describing what it communicates or how it was made.
AC9AMAFP01.typical_width: Present arts works to peers in gallery, performance, or digital formats; use positive language to comment on their own and others' works; explain features, themes or process choices when asked; engage with audience responses.
wider: Use digital devices to record and curate a sequence of images documenting an arts exploration; add commentary expressing feelings, emotions and understandings about the work and the process
Present a retelling of a story (through dramatic play, puppets, or digital capture) to another class or community audience, introducing the work and describing favourite moments
Participate in a class gallery or performance walk — share work, comment on peers' work using observational language (similarities, differences, use of materials, elements of design)
elaborations: sharing their artworks with the class via a "gallery" or "performance walk"
performing songs, soundscapes or chants/raps, using music skills they have learnt and practised
taking images of class arts events (with permission from the people involved), creating an image sequence to document the occasion, and adding sound
talking about ideas such as themes, processes used to make the work, or features of the work such as patterns, pathways or lines
presenting retellings of stories to peers; for example, through dramatic play using repurposed objects, toys or puppets they have made
sharing their work with their teacher and responding to questions such as "What is going on in your work?", "Tell me the story of what is happening?", "What did you enjoy about making this work?"
performing movement/dance sequences they have created for other groups in their class
using digital devices to record their arts explorations; for example, curating (selecting, ordering) a sequence of digital images (photos) to show the steps in a process
